report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **supported by clinical evidence**. Anti-cytokine therapies significantly reduce depressive symptoms in individuals with chronic inflammatory conditions.

### Summary of Evidence
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials involving patients with chronic inflammatory illnesses (such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease) demonstrate that anti-cytokine treatments—including monoclonal antibodies and specific cytokine inhibitors—exhibit significant antidepressant activity compared to placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/, https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167). 

Broader investigations into immunomodulatory treatments support these findings, showing that targeting key inflammatory cytokine pathways leads to clinically meaningful reductions in depressive symptom severity (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7244402/). Furthermore, evidence indicates that monoclonal antibodies hold substantial promise for treating depressive symptoms co-morbid with physical inflammatory disorders, with mood improvements occurring beyond the indirect effects of physical symptom relief alone (https://www.psychiatrist.com/jcp/immune-targeted-therapies-depression-antidepressant-effects-monoclonal-antibodies/).
